hints: Rewrite the expression as $(\sin\theta)^{-2}$ and apply the chain rule.
Differentiate the outer power first, then multiply by $\cos\theta$; express the result using either sine and cosine or cosecant and cotangent.
walkthrough:
Write the expression $\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}$ in power form:
$$y = (\sin\theta)^{-2}$$

Apply the chain rule $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\left(u^{-2}\right) = -2u^{-3}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}\theta}$ with $u = \sin\theta$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \cos\theta$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = -2(\sin\theta)^{-3}\cos\theta = -\dfrac{2\cos\theta}{\sin^3\theta}$$

Alternatively, write in terms of cosecant and cotangent functions:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}(\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta) = 2\operatorname{cosec}\theta(-\operatorname{cosec}\theta\cot\theta) = -2\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta\cot\theta$$

hints: Rearrange the differential equation to separate $x$ from the trigonometric functions of $\theta$.
Use the derivative from part (i) to integrate the trigonometric side, and include a constant.
Apply $x=4$ at $\theta=\pi/6$, then choose the positive square root because $x>0$.
walkthrough:
Separate variables by isolating terms in $x$ and $\theta$:
$$x\tan\theta\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = -\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$$
$$x\,\mathrm{d}x = -\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta}{\tan\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Express the right-hand side in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$:
$$-\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta}{\tan\theta} = -\dfrac{1/\sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta/\cos\theta} = -\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin^3\theta}$$

Integrate both sides:
$$\int x\,\mathrm{d}x = \int -\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin^3\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$
$$\dfrac{1}{2}x^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\right) + C = \dfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta + C$$

Multiply through by $2$ and let $c = 2C$:
$$x^2 = \operatorname{cosec}^2\theta + c$$

Substitute the given boundary condition $\theta = \dfrac{1}{6}\pi$ and $x = 4$:
$$\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\pi\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \implies \operatorname{cosec}\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\pi\right) = 2$$
$$4^2 = 2^2 + c$$
$$16 = 4 + c \implies c = 12$$

Substitute $c = 12$ back into the equation:
$$x^2 = \operatorname{cosec}^2\theta + 12 \quad \left(\text{or } x^2 = \dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta} + 12\right)$$

Take the positive square root since $x > 0$:
$$x = \sqrt{\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta + 12} \quad \left(\text{or } x = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta} + 12}\right)$$
